articles.title: Unlearnt lessons of history
articles.content: TODAY, the country’s hybrid government is fixated onaltering Pakistan’s constitutionally mandated provincial structureand multiplying administrative units. To sell the idea, establishment apologists have rolled out some disingenuous arguments. They claim this will improve governance and miraculously solve the country’s problems overnight. A debate has been generated in the media about the pros and cons of administrative changes and breaking provinces into more units. Parliament has yet to discuss this. That is unsurprising. Deliberation is not this legislature’s strong suit. It has rushed through constitutional amendments in record time, once in the dead of night and without meaningful debate. Meanwhile, speculation is mounting that another constitutional amendment is being prepared to push through ‘administrative changes’. Absent from the establishment’s consideration of these sweeping changes are lessons from Pakistan’s history. Over the decades, the country’s rulers have experimented with parliamentary, presidential, semi-presidential, quasi-parliamentary systems, direct military rule, and more recently a hybrid model, which involves informal power-sharing between the military and civilians, with the former as dominant partner. Pakistan has tried them all. Yet each switch only contributed to political instability. The only system to command legitimacy and broad support is parliamentary democracy, despite the fact that parliamentary supremacy over the executive has never been realised. Linked to these experiments has been the status and rights of provinces in a federal system. As the provincial configuration and federating units largely coincided with the ethnic composition of people of each province, the need was always felt to make federalism a reality, not just a constitutional precept to ensure the people of all four provinces felt they were part of an inclusive and fair system. Pakistan’s troubled history offers a cautionary lesson against altering the provincial structure. But the federal structure and provincial rights have always been contested issues in Pakistan’s history. Contested on many counts. Smaller provinces have long resented Punjab’s political hegemony, sought greater powers and autonomy and felt the distribution of resources has been unfair. Unelected institutions have always preferred a centralised polity while military rule meant the country functioned as a virtual unitary state. Long periods of unrepresentative rule fuelled alienation among the smaller provinces by marginalising them, suppressing regional identities, concentrating power at the centre and weakening federalism. The creation of One Unit in the 1950s, which merged all the provinces of what was then West Pakistan into a single unit, was aimed at creating ‘parity’ with the more populous eastern wing of the country to undercut its numerical majority. This politically motivated project imposed a unitary system and all but destroyed the country’s federal character. It was justified by totally false and frivolous arguments. They included claims it would end “provincial prejudices”, reduce administrative expenses and help develop backward areas. The move had disastrous consequences. It fanned the flames of nationalist and regionalist sentiment in the smaller provinces of West Pakistan and strengthened centrifugal forces across the country. It contributed to the sense of discrimination among the people of East Pakistan that, along with other factors, found expression in the Bengali nationalist movement and ultimately led to the break-up of Pakistan in 1971. The issue of provincial rights continued to be a source of tensions and contestation. The 1973 Constitution struck a delicate balance between the centre and provinces in a multiethnic state, assured provincial autonomy and enjoined reciprocal obligations between the federating units. Unfortunately, this was observed more in its breach than in its adherence. Opposition-run provincial governments were ousted in the 1970s by prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. This reinforced a political tradition that began in the early years after independence when provincial governments were summarily dismissed by the central government. This seriously undermined national unity. These and other actions widened interprovincial disparities, deepened alienation among smaller provinces and led to the insurgency in Balochistan in the 1970s. This intensified during the 2000s but their antecedents reached back to the 1950s. The insurgency continues today as a result of monumental mishandling of the province and Baloch sentiment by successive governments. Authoritarian measures also gave a fillip to Pakhtun nationalism, even though over time this waned with the increasing representation of KP in the country’s power elite and bureaucracy. The troubled history of federalism and provincial tensions in Pakistan offers a cautionary lesson against altering the country’s four ethnically distinct provinces. Past attempts to do that or erode constitutionally guaranteed provincial rights only widened fault lines and created new ones. These efforts were never about better governance or a stronger administrative system. They were about control. They reflected the interests of a ruling elite seeking to entrench political dominance, with little regard for national unity and cohesion. The same logic applies to those in the current hybrid government pushing to create new provinces and fragment existing ones. This is about control, not reform. True ethnic minorities in some provinces, such as Seraiki speakers in southern Punjab, have long wanted their own province. Some political parties have actively supported this. But the challenge is how to square this with carving out a new unit that could undermine the delicate constitutional balance, spark controversy and encourage others to demand new provinces. The18th Constitutional Amendment, backed by all parties in 2010, opened a new chapter in provincial empowerment. Over a dozen ministries were devolved from the federal level to the provinces. But this also raised capacity issues and whether provinces could handle the increased fiscal power and resources devolved to them. The fiscal aspect evoked the most criticism. Because with the 2009 National Finance Commission award, the substantial transfer of resources to the provinces left the federal government unable to meet its financial obligations. While this tussle over revenue needs to be resolved and provinces should mobilise their own resources, creating smaller provinces or rolling back the amendment is not the answer. In fact, the rationale for redrawing provincial boundaries remains opaque. This lack of clarity reinforces the impression that the motive is to increase control, not to improve governance. If we want real reform, it’s not by carving out new provinces. It’s by empowering local government. The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
articles.author: Maleeha Lodhi

articles.title: Women’s leadership
articles.content: PAKISTAN doesn’t fare well on indices related to gender gap and women’s empowerment. The damning statistics include the number of girls who are out of school, the wide gender digital divide, high rates of violence against women, and women’s low representation in private and public leadership positions. However, over time, there have been significant advances for Pakistani women leaders. Mohammad Ali Jinnah’s sister,Fatima Jinnah, was a key figure in Pakistan’s independence movement. She later became a presidential candidate, derided by the dictator Gen Ayub Khan. WhenBenazir Bhuttowas elected prime minister in 1988, Pakistan became the first Muslim-majority country to be led by a woman. Pakistani women have led movements against dictators, including generals Ayub, Zia and Musharraf. Asma Jahangir was the first woman to be elected president of the Supreme Court Bar Association. Begum Naseem Wali Khan was the first woman to win a general election seat in the country.Justice Ayesha Malikis the first woman Supreme Court judge. Currently,Maryam Nawazis the first woman chief minister in Pakistan. Trans women have also made their mark, with Aisha Mughal being the first to represent a country at a UN session. Recently,Nayyab Aliwas nominated for a civilian award by the government. But despite these significant positives, the prosecution of political women in Pakistan is at an all-time high. Several women leaders of the PTI remain behind bars, including the ageing cancer survivor, Dr Yasmin Rashid, who hashealth issues. Since January, award-winning human rights lawyer Imaan Mazari Hazir has been in jailserving a 17-year sentencefor mere tweets. Baloch women have now joined numerous men who have been forcibly disappeared; several remain in jail in politically motivated cases. The prosecution of political women in the country is at an all-time high. Do such incarcerations, cases and disappearances send an encouraging message to young girls across Pakistan? Does it motivate reluctant families to send girls to school so they can get an education and start careers? Does it motivate young lawyers to take up cases of the voiceless pro bono? Does it encourage young women to enter politics and do good for the people? The incarcerations reflect a deep-rooted patriarchy that plagues the entire system. Take, for instance, gender-based attacks against women during election campaigns. The Digital Rights Foundation documented at least 163 social media posts in the run-up to the 2024 election that included gendered disinformation against women politicians, and at least 47 posts targeting “journalists covering the elections, subjecting them to gendered insults and online trolling campaigns that included online threats of physical assault”. Deepfakes targeting women human rights defenders have become commonplace, with dehumanising content being disseminated online of women that are critical of state policies, with little to no consequences for such actions — despite Section 22 of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act that makes edited and non-consensual imagery a crime. Since the2025 amendment to Peca, the state is an eager complainant against journalists who are critical of it. Whereas the new ability of the state to file cybercrime cases against activists, journalists and politicians is to be condemned and should be reversed; it is worth noting that the state doesn’t take cognisance of instances of harassment and vitriol on social media that lead to crimes against women and children. This includes routine cases of men mercilessly killing women for rejecting their advances and proposals. The victims include women who are public figures on social media platforms as content creators. On Aug 20, former professor and motivational speaker Faisal Asghar Imam wasnamed in the murder caseof his wife in their home, and social media was rife with testimonies of him making his students uncomfortable in class and online. The link between online misogyny and physical harm to life must not be taken lightly. When Peca was being promulgated, those of us who opposed it were labelled anti-women for opposing the law. Today, we see how women are harassed, jailed, and punished including for naming their harassers by the same law meant to protect them. The abuse of the law is not restricted to targeting women who dare to speak truth to power. Human rights lawyer Hadi Ali Chattha is currently serving a 17-year sentence for supporting his wife Imaan Mazari Hazir, with his punishment framed for the “crime” of reposting her tweets. Seemingly, men who support women related to them, they too will be punished. In our geopolitical context, targeting women in the public sphere is particularly alarming. Girls in Afghanistan are not allowed to go to school after Class 6; women are not allowed to leave their house for employment, and they cannot even sing or be heard in public. In Iran, women have been killed for simply opposing the state’s enforcement of head covering rules. In such an environment, it would be a powerful message to the neighbourhood if Pakistan has women in positions of power. Sadly, the current women’s leadership in Pakistan is hardly representative of half the population. There are no women federal ministers, and only one woman minister of state. In Sindh, the PPP that brought us a woman prime minister has only two women cabinet members; while the party’s cabinet in Balochistan has only one woman minister. In KP, the PTI has no women in the cabinet. A woman chief minister leads Punjab, but her cabinet has only two women ministers, with Marriyum Aurangzeb holding six portfolios. As a pluralist federal democracy, at least on paper, Pakistan must move in line with Article 25 of the Constitution that empowers the government to make special provisions to protect women and children, apart from ensuring equal treatment for them. Women political prisoners, along with men, must be released; and women being half the population must be given half of the governing share. We owe this to every young girl in Pakistan. The writer is director of Bolo Bhi, an advocacy forum for digital rights.
articles.author: Usama Khilji

articles.title: Zombie writers
articles.content: LESS than two months before he died from cancer, American writer John Cheever, his now-disgraced biographer tells us, accepted the National Medal for Literature. He had to hobble across the stage with the help of his wife, months of cancer treatment having left him “pitifully frail”. Yet his motto was intact: that literature was salvation of the damned. “A page of good prose,” he told his cheering audience, “remains invincible.” Remembered fellow author John Updike, “All the literary acolytes assembled there fell quite silent, astonished by such faith.” Fast-forward to the present: the smartphone is grafted to our hands; our eyeballs are fused to the short video format; and we all feel the need to upload pictures of breakfast for the viewing pleasure of neo-Nazis in the comments section. But whatever the hazards of this alien invasion, its main flying saucer has now landed: ChatGPT. Then Gemini. Then Claude. We were told this final boss, artificial intelligence, was inevitable; that our own thoughts could safely be farmed out to robots. It was the same way the internet killed the newspaper, because print was dead. When YouTube mauled network television because the media was corrupt. When Grok and Elon gutted Twitter because race riots were respectable again. For a while now, we have been witness to this great debasement of human thought. But ever since chatbots and their billionaire bosses have come for writing itself, we stand to lose the most vital part of ourselves. Consider:AI does not feel. It does not dream (though it does, we are told, hallucinate). A study of personal statements from 370,000 students tells us that after ChatGPT appeared, essays had smoother language but lacked creativity. A separate study found that human-written essays offered up to eight times more new ideas, whereas even short stories were far richer in their offbeat magic. A lot of this is because of how our brains work: to be human is to connect two seemingly unrelated subjects, based, as one educationist wrote, on linking “unique personal experiences”. A racetrack could mean an old friend; a song the death of a loved one. But machines, on the other hand, generate words divorced from thought. They predict words that are best placed to complete a sentence, based on the books that have been pulped to train them. That is, after all, the essence of AI writing: authorship without intention. As far back as 1964, “the first book of free verse written by an electronic computer” was published in Montreal with such gems as, “The apple shapes the world, but the rain enhances the grapes” — AI slop’s noble ancestor. That’s not to say it hasn’t its uses, if in the right doses: coding, translation, synthesis, data-crunching, infographics, customer service. It’s good for the despised work email, the Excel spreadsheet. It is, at its best, a semi-competent sounding board: not for no reason has AI slop colonised every last post on LinkedIn, that other land of brutal banality. But what a disaster for students to outsource the single most beautiful outcome of education — critical thought — to this glorified calculator (‘We just use it for proofing and professionalising our own drafts,’ they always say, forgetting that the real skill, for coherence of thought, has always been revision). What a waste that countries must run dry because the office intern can’t teach himself how to spell ‘carbon dioxide’. And what intellectual dishonesty for grownups to claim a robot’s drivel as their own in essays, speeches, and publications in general. If the author cannot respect their audience enough to do the hard work of thinking through what they wish to express, then the audience needn’t respect the author with their time and attention either. Send us the prompts you put in instead. We’ll read those. I think, therefore I am. If there’s a modern equivalent, it is: I generate, therefore I consume. But if I consume far more than I create, then that may be getting the whole point of existence backwards. Might we return to the business of real life; to the leaves on the trees? To human connection? To go back to where we began, AI cannot mimic John Cheever’s writing style beyond a vapid ghost of the original, because it is only the original that lets the reader touch midlife’s misted glass, or feel the bracing need for a redemption just beyond reach. His journals, whenever someone stumbles across them, are a revelation. As The Paris Review put it, “How thrilling to discover … this offhand, extemporising masterpiece, a storehouse of incomparable lyricism — no one writes light or water or fire better than Cheever — commingled with the greatest index of shame in American letters.” No chatbot could have written that sentence. It’s a human being telling us what another human being meant to him. The writer is an advocate of the Supreme Court.
articles.author: Asad Rahim Khan

articles.title: Empty promises
articles.content: SYSTEMS collapse when promises are not honoured. In a democracy, institutional health is measured by how each branch — legislature, executive and judiciary — upholds its commitments. One such commitment is to conduct elections within 90 days of the dissolution of an assembly as required by the Constitution. Commitments exist for the collective good. They collapse when they are negotiated to secure personal or institutional ambitions — such as when a law is tailored to protect the tenure of the chief justice. Democracy, as currently practised, is designed in a way that cultivates a kind of collective inanity. Representatives surrender their own thinking, and the promises they made to the people, to the party; the parties, in turn, obey the whip and toe the line. Truth is not considered valuable in and of itself; it is a tool in a box, taken out when useful and put away when not. This can be seen in the 26th and 27th Amendments, and the Peca and NAB amendments, each tied by its defenders to the ‘public good’. Those who supported these laws gave more importance to optics that would present them in a favourable light, than to truth itself. Against what standard, then, should these promises be measured? Political and economic stability rests on a fairly simple premise: legislatures exist to enact laws that promote peace and security. The role of the executive is to create an environment where people are not afraid of voicing their concerns. The role of the judicial branch is to ensure that the system rests on justice, and not oppression. Measure the promises made against these standards to see where we actually stand and at what point the system collapsed. But that is hard to ascertain when the language we use around politics and economics has grown hollow and vague — and our thinking along with it. George Orwell made a related point in his essay Politics and the English Language. He argued that the language we use around economics and politics has become hollow, flatter and vaguer, and our thinking about politics and economics, too, has become flatter and vaguer with it. When we are asked for our opinion on an issue, Orwell says, we are handed a menu of clichés and readymade platitudes, and we limit ourselves to rattling these off. A leader can say ‘the system has collapsed’ — a sentence constructed to sound like an admission while holding no one accountable. The question is — whose system has collapsed, and at whose hands? A government will announce ‘negative growth’, instead of admitting a recession, because the euphemism does the work the truth is not permitted to do. Why has the system collapsed and at whose hands? The Constitution — a social contract — ought to be upheld by those tasked with implementing it. Any contract dies the moment one party stops honouring it. Ghalib wrote: “Qatre mein dijla dikhai na de aur juzv mein kul/ Khel larkon ka hua, deeda-i-beena na hua.” If the river cannot be seen in the drop, if the whole cannot be found in its smallest part, then this is not insight but a child’s game. A missed deadline, continuous disregard of judicial pronouncements, a compromised electoral system, a mandate believed to be stolen — these are not separate failures to be tallied. Each one reflects a total collapse, visible in a single drop, for those willing to actually see it. Sanctity of promises constitutes the bedrock of society. It is what makes or breaks a relationship. The trust of our citizens has been eroded so many times that changing words in the Constitution now means little, when what was needed was to uphold the document in the first place. An environment is now being created for further constitutional amendments, sought through the same people who broke the last set of promises. That we allow this cycle to repeat itself is not merely a failure of politics; it is a failure to look ahead. Kant identified why we so rarely see clearly enough to demand better. In his essay on enlightenment, he wrote that human beings remain in a self-imposed immaturity, mainly out of cowardice and laziness, unable to use their own understanding without another’s guidance. We have outsourced our thinking, and our belief, to the people we follow and the technology we depend on. Praising the interior minister for saying, on camera, what was once only said in drawing rooms is nothing more than silliness. This attitude mistakes candour about dishonesty for honesty itself. What we need is not a minister admitting what is said behind closed doors, nor another amendment. We need to respect our people and to honour the promises made to them in the Constitution.
articles.author: Sufiyan Bin Muneer

articles.title: ‘Grand dialogue’
articles.content: THE country’stop civil and military leadersare absolutely right when they say that dialogue and development are needed to address Balochistan’s crises. But perhaps one should recall that many earlier attempts by the state to bring peace to the province were stalled or remain unimplemented. In order to truly stabilise Balochistan and bring lasting peace to this troubled province, a credible political process must begin, with the state guaranteeing that it will fully implement previous promises, as well as new agreements. While speaking at the Balochistan National Workshop in Islamabad recently, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for a “grand, frank and meaningful dialogue” to address the province’s issues. He added that the province’s people had first right over its resources. In a similar vein the chief of defence forces stressed the need for empowering Balochistan’s youth. It is certainly welcome that the rulers see the need to tackle Balochistan’s political problems through dialogue. While kinetic measures are needed to deal with immediate terrorist threats, the underlying factors fuelling discontent can only be handled through a political process. The state must keep in mind previous attempts to address the province’s problems. For example, the PPP government had in 2009 launched theAghaz-i-Huqooq-i-Balochistanpackage. Despite the passage of 17 years, many of the package’s key points remain unimplemented. For example, it had proposed releasing political workers, except those involved in heinous crimes. However, over the past few months, we have seen peaceful activists rounded up and thrown in jail. Similarly, the 2009 package had sought to address the province’s socioeconomic woes; suffice it to say, social indicators in Balochistan remain miserable. The PML-N had launched a package of its own in 2015. Much of that scheme also remains unfulfilled. CPEC was similarly supposed to transform the province’s fortunes. It has not. Instead of reinventing the wheel, the state must implement what it had promised in these packages. Many of these schemes’ salient points reflect the demands of the province’s nationalist politicians. Therefore, to implement these promises in full, a grand dialogue should bring on board the province’s genuine political leadership, as well as peaceful activists, while a verifiable and transparent mechanism needs to be worked out to help implement previous and new promises. The past few months have seen asharp spike in terrorist activity in Balochistan. The only sustainable way of addressing the insurgency is to supplement kinetic actions with a genuine political process that can, in the long-term, eliminate the underlying factors that are fuelling discontent.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Privatisation push
articles.content: THE privatisation programme seems to be moving forward — finally. Eleven prospective investors have now submitted expressions of interest for Gepco following a similarly strong response for Fesco earlier this month, with Iesco’s deadline still to come in September. The PIA sale appears to have supplied the push this programme needed — proof that the government is ready to wash its hands of businesses it should not have involved itself in. What makes the Discos’ response more encouraging than PIA’s is who is showing up. Turkish and Saudi investors are in the mix for both Gepco and Fesco, and Fesco separately drew Chinese interest — a foreign presence PIA’s privatisation could not attract. Add a list of big domestic companies and the field looks genuinely competitive rather than a formality staged for the government’s benefit. None of that guarantees that interest will convert into bids the government is hoping for. The investor feedback report the Privatisation Commission compiled after its roadshows in Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and China reads more like a conditions list. Investors want the multi-year tariff control period stretched from five years to seven to 10, arguing that distribution assets with decades-long lives cannot be financed against a five-year regulatory horizon. They want tariffs tied to individual Disco performance rather than the current uniform structure, which effectively taxes efficient operators to subsidise inefficient ones. They want binding protection against tariffs or contracts being reopened later by a government or a court, a fear rooted in our history of renegotiating deals after the fact. And they want a regulator that can actually make faster decisions, have clearer enforcement powers but enjoy less discretion to intervene unpredictably. These are not cosmetic asks. They go to the heart of whether Pakistan’s regulatory institutions can credibly commit to arrangements that outlast the political cycle in which they are signed. If the government treats these concerns as bargaining noise to be managed rather than structural gaps to be fixed, the interest recorded this month may thin out by the time actual bids are due. But if it uses this feedback to extend the tariff regime, build real regulatory independence and put contractual guarantees beyond the reach of future reversal, the payoff will extend well past the power sector.
articles.author: Editorial
